rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Tables 2-7 report the authors' own long-term field experiment (2010-19) in a Sicilian orange orchard with FI, SDI, RDI and PRD treatments, measuring stem water potential, sap flow, soil water content, yield, fruit quality and water use efficiency over the 2018-19 seasons.
rows.notes: The study is a primary field experiment, but it tests deficit irrigation strategies (sustained deficit, regulated deficit, partial root-zone drying) under surface/sub-surface drip, not app-based or 'smart' irrigation scheduling. Irrigation was scheduled with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method adjusted by crop/localisation coefficients and soil moisture probes, which is a conventional agronomic scheduling procedure rather than an app or decision-support tool. What the study actually shows is that after a decade of deficit irrigation the orange trees achieved yield and fruit quality similar to full irrigation while saving up to ~50-53% of irrigation water and reaching 2.6-3.1 times higher WUE in PRD (Tables 5-7). Climate-change adaptation/risk management is only invoked as framing in the Introduction and Conclusion (water scarcity in semi-arid Mediterranean areas); no result links an app-scheduling technology to resilience or risk reduction. Hence Q2 is 'no' and Q3-Q9 follow as 'no'.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study concerns deficit irrigation adaptation of citrus trees; it does not evaluate an app-based or smart irrigation scheduling technology, so the review's attribution to 'smart irrigation' is a loose grouping under 'water-saving technologies'.
